What Polarization Looks Like
•  Judges cultural difference as "us vs. them"
•  Defense: my cultural practices are superior
•  Reversal: other cultures are superior to mine
•  Uses stereotypes to simplify cultural groups
•  Discomfort with cultural difference triggers evaluation
Your Developmental Goal
Begin searching for commonalities alongside differences. Move from evaluating cultural difference to being curious about it. Judgment is the current default — curiosity is the next step.
2 / 13 1
Tutorial 1 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Understanding Your IDI Results
What Polarization Means — Defense, Reversal, and the "Us vs. Them" Mindset
Why This Matters
Polarization is a judgmental orientation that sees cultural difference through an "us vs. them" lens. It shows up as Defense (my culture is superior) or Reversal (other cultures are superior). Both are ethnocentric — and both are addressable.
Learner Goals
Accurately describe the Polarization orientation and its two sub-types: Defense and Reversal
Identify which sub-type is more prominent in your own IDI profile
Accept your results as a developmental starting point rather than a moral judgment
Developmental Activity
Reflection Journal: Write 3–5 sentences describing a situation where you noticed yourself thinking "that's just wrong" or "they do it so much better than we do" about a cultural practice. Which sub-type — Defense or Reversal — does that reaction most resemble?
Reflection Question
What emotions came up when you saw your IDI score? How does it feel to have your judgments about other cultures named and measured?
Facilitator Note
Normalize Polarization as the most common orientation after Denial. About 16% of people score here. Emphasize that noticing cultural difference is genuine developmental progress — the work now is moving from judgment to curiosity.
3 / 13 2
Tutorial 2 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Recognizing the "Us vs. Them" Pattern
Seeing Polarization in Your Own Thinking and Behavior
Why This Matters
People in Polarization often don't recognize their own evaluative lens. They experience their judgments as simply "seeing things clearly." The developmental move is learning to catch the evaluative framing in real time.
Learner Goals
Identify at least three ways "us vs. them" thinking shows up in your daily work
Distinguish between observing cultural difference and evaluating it
Name one recurring situation where you apply a judgmental frame to cultural difference
Developmental Activity
Judgment Audit: For one week, keep a brief log of moments when you catch yourself using evaluative language about cultural difference — words like "wrong," "better," "primitive," "oversensitive," or "superior." Note the trigger, the thought, and what cultural group it was directed at.
Reflection Question
When you evaluate another cultural practice as inferior or superior, whose standard are you using as the baseline? Where did that standard come from?
Facilitator Note
Do not shame evaluative thinking — it is a natural cognitive response to noticing difference. The goal is metacognitive awareness: helping the learner observe their own judgments as data, not as truth.
4 / 13 3
Tutorial 3 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Understanding Defense
When "My Way" Feels Like the Only Right Way
Why This Matters
Defense is characterized by an uncritical view of one's own culture and an overly critical view of others. It can manifest as stereotyping, resistance to change, and discomfort when cultural norms are challenged. Understanding it without shame is the first step past it.
Learner Goals
Define the Defense sub-type and describe how it manifests in professional settings
Identify at least two ways Defense shows up in your own work context
Explain why Defense feels "normal" and "correct" to the person experiencing it
Developmental Activity
Defense Mapping: List 3–5 cultural practices or communication styles that you find genuinely irritating, inefficient, or wrong in your workplace. For each one, ask: Is this actually harmful — or is it simply different from what I am used to? What does that distinction reveal?
Reflection Question
What cultural practices or values do you hold as "just the right way to do things"? What would it mean if those are preferences shaped by your own background, not universal standards?
Facilitator Note
Be especially attentive to learners who frame Defense as "just having standards" or "being realistic." That framing is itself Defense. Gently surface the cultural assumption behind the standard without triggering defensiveness.
5 / 13 4
Tutorial 4 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Understanding Reversal
When "Their Way" Always Seems Better Than Mine
Why This Matters
Reversal flips the polarity of Defense — one's own culture is seen as inferior or problematic, while other cultures are idealized. This orientation is equally ethnocentric because it still operates from a binary judgment framework rather than genuine cultural complexity.
Learner Goals
Define the Reversal sub-type and explain why it is still an ethnocentric orientation
Describe how Reversal can masquerade as cultural humility or allyship
Identify at least one way Reversal may show up in your own professional perspective
Developmental Activity
Reversal Reflection: Think of a cultural group you tend to idealize or romanticize. Write a short paragraph: What do you assume is better about their approach? What might you be oversimplifying or ignoring? Who in that group might push back on your idealized view?
Reflection Question
What is the difference between genuinely appreciating another culture's strengths and using that culture as a critique of your own? Why does the distinction matter?
Facilitator Note
Reversal is common among equity practitioners and people with strong social justice commitments. Frame the developmental move as building more complex appreciation — not abandoning values, but replacing simplistic inversion with genuine nuance.
6 / 13 5
Tutorial 5 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Polarization in the Disability Services Context
How "Us vs. Them" Shows Up in Equity and Service Work at DSD
Why This Matters
In disability services and equity work, Polarization can be especially costly. Defense can drive paternalistic service delivery; Reversal can lead to over-correction or inappropriate generalization. Both undermine authentic partnership with the communities DSD serves.
Learner Goals
Identify two ways Defense or Reversal may affect service interactions or team dynamics at DSD
Describe how Polarization can masquerade as either advocacy or professional rigor
Connect Polarization awareness to the One DSD commitment to equitable outcomes
Developmental Activity
Scenario Analysis: Review two brief case scenarios — one illustrating Defense in a service interaction, one illustrating Reversal. For each: What is the cultural judgment being made? Who is harmed by it? What would a more developmentally advanced response look like?
Reflection Question
In your current role, are there groups of colleagues, clients, or communities that you hold in lower regard — or in uncritical higher regard — based on cultural identity? What is the impact of that stance on your work?
Facilitator Note
This is the bridge module. Connect Polarization explicitly to the equity mission. Both Defense and Reversal are barriers to authentic partnership. The goal is culturally informed, non-judgmental practice — not "diversity theater."
7 / 13 6
Tutorial 6 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Finding Commonality Across Difference
The Bridge Skill: Searching for Shared Goals and Values
Why This Matters
The developmental move from Polarization toward Minimization involves beginning to look for commonalities alongside differences. This is not about erasing difference — it is about recognizing shared humanity as a foundation for cross-cultural relationship.
Learner Goals
Identify at least three genuine commonalities you share with a cultural group you have previously judged
Distinguish between false universalism (ignoring difference) and genuine commonality (building connection)
Practice finding shared goals with someone whose cultural background differs from your own
Developmental Activity
Common Ground Interview: Identify a colleague or community member from a cultural background different from your own — ideally one you have held judgments about. Have a conversation focused entirely on shared goals, values, or challenges. Afterward, write: What surprised you? What shifted?
Reflection Question
Is it possible to recognize genuine shared humanity without erasing the real differences that shape people's experiences? What does that balance look like in practice?
Facilitator Note
This is a bridge activity between Polarization and Minimization. Common-ground work is developmentally appropriate here — it softens judgment without yet demanding the full complexity of Acceptance. Move gradually.
8 / 13 7
Tutorial 7 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Interrupting Stereotypes in Real Time
Moving from Generalizations to Genuine Curiosity
Why This Matters
Polarization relies heavily on stereotypes — oversimplified, evaluative generalizations about cultural groups. Learning to catch and interrupt stereotyping in real time is one of the most practical developmental skills at this orientation.
Learner Goals
Define stereotype and explain how it functions differently from a cultural generalization
Identify two stereotypes you hold — consciously or unconsciously — about a cultural group
Practice replacing a stereotyped assumption with a genuinely curious question
Developmental Activity
Stereotype Interrupt: Pick one cultural group you hold assumptions about. Write down 3 things you "know" about that group. Then: (1) Where did each belief come from? (2) How certain are you? (3) What question could you ask instead of assuming? Bring your reflection to your next check-in.
Reflection Question
How does holding a stereotype — even a positive one — reduce your ability to see an individual person clearly? What do you lose when you generalize?
Facilitator Note
Be sensitive to the shame response here. Many learners at Polarization have been told their stereotyping is wrong but not helped to understand why or how to move past it. Focus on the cognitive mechanism, not moral condemnation.
9 / 13 8
Tutorial 8 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Managing the Discomfort of Cultural Difference
Using Discomfort as a Signal, Not a Verdict
Why This Matters
In Polarization, cultural difference triggers discomfort, anxiety, or threat — which the mind resolves by judging the other as inferior (Defense) or the self as inferior (Reversal). Learning to tolerate discomfort without immediately resolving it through judgment is a core developmental skill.
Learner Goals
Identify your personal emotional triggers in cross-cultural interactions
Explain why discomfort around cultural difference does not mean the other person is wrong
Practice one discomfort-tolerance strategy in a real cross-cultural interaction this week
Developmental Activity
Discomfort Mapping: Think of a recent cross-cultural interaction that felt uncomfortable. Describe: What triggered the discomfort? What judgment did you reach? What would it look like to stay in the discomfort long enough to get curious instead of evaluating?
Reflection Question
What would change in your work — and your relationships — if you responded to cultural discomfort with curiosity rather than judgment?
Facilitator Note
Somatic awareness is useful here. Discomfort often registers physically before it becomes a conscious judgment. Helping learners notice the body cue — and pause before evaluating — is a practical, high-leverage skill.
10 / 13 9
Tutorial 9 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Building Your Intercultural Development Plan
Setting Intentional Goals to Move from Judgment to Curiosity
Why This Matters
Moving from Polarization toward Minimization requires structured, intentional effort — not just willingness. An Intercultural Development Plan (IDP) translates awareness into concrete developmental action with real accountability.
Learner Goals
Draft a personal IDP with at least two specific, measurable growth goals for the next 90 days
Identify at least one professional situation per week where you can practice interrupting judgment
Establish a check-in structure with your Qualified Administrator or accountability partner
Developmental Activity
IDP Draft: Complete the following — (1) My primary developmental goal for the next 90 days is... (2) The specific situation where I will practice is... (3) I will know I am making progress when... (4) The judgment pattern I most need to interrupt is... (5) My accountability structure is...
Reflection Question
What conditions at work — team dynamics, time pressure, leadership behavior — make it harder to practice moving past Polarization? What support do you need?
Facilitator Note
IDPs for Polarization should focus on specific, recurring situations — not abstract commitments. The more precisely the learner can name the trigger and the desired alternative response, the more effective the plan will be.
11 / 13 10
Tutorial 10 of 10  ·  Polarization → Minimization
Moving Toward Minimization
A Developmental Bridge to the Next Orientation
Why This Matters
As judgment softens, learners in Polarization will begin to emphasize commonalities and universal values — this is the Minimization orientation emerging. It feels like progress and is progress, even though Minimization brings its own blind spots. Preparing learners for this transition prevents overconfidence.
Learner Goals
Describe the Minimization orientation and how it differs from Polarization
Explain why moving into Minimization is a step forward — and what its new developmental challenge will be
Identify two early signs that your Polarization is beginning to soften
Developmental Activity
Continuum Mapping: Draw your own version of the IDC. Mark where you are now (Polarization — Defense, Reversal, or both). Mark where you want to be in 12 months. In between, write 3–5 "bridge moments" — specific experiences, insights, or practices that will carry you forward.
Reflection Question
As the "us vs. them" frame softens, what new challenges might emerge? What might you start to overlook or de-emphasize that still matters?
Facilitator Note
Celebrate the softening of judgment explicitly. A learner who is beginning to notice commonalities and feeling less reactive to difference is genuinely developing. Flag the Minimization risk early so they are prepared — not surprised — when they get there.
12 / 13 Your Path Forward
From Judgment to Curiosity — A Summary
01
Name the Pattern
Identify whether you lean Defense, Reversal, or both. Awareness is the start.
02
Catch Judgments
Notice evaluative thinking in real time. Log it — don't shame it.
03
Find Commonality
Practice searching for shared goals before focusing on differences.
04
Interrupt Bias
Replace assumptions with genuine questions. Get specific.
05
Use Your IDP
Use your plan. Every intentional practice builds the next orientation.
